claims.claim: A sheet of paper won't fit between the stones of Sacsayhuamán
claims.quote: The stones are so closely spaced that a single piece of paper will not fit between many of the stones.

claims.claim: Sacsayhuamán's walls are dry stone, laid without mortar
claims.quote: Dry stone walls constructed of huge stones were built on the site, with the workers carefully cutting the boulders to fit them together tightly without mortar.

claims.claim: Sacsayhuamán is above/north of Cusco
claims.quote: is a citadel on the northern outskirts of the city of Cusco, Peru, the historic capital of the Inca Empire

claims.claim: The walls lean inward
claims.quote: the variety of their interlocking shapes, and the way the walls lean inward

claims.claim: Rounded corners, interlocking shapes and the inward lean are thought to have helped the ruins survive Cuzco's earthquakes
claims.quote: This precision, combined with the rounded corners of the blocks, the variety of their interlocking shapes, and the way the walls lean inward, is thought to have helped the ruins survive devastating earthquakes in Cuzco.

claims.claim: The largest block weighs up to 200 tonnes; estimates run from 128 tonnes to almost 200
claims.quote: Estimates for the weight of the largest Limestone block vary from 128 tonnes to almost 200 tonnes.

claims.claim: The stone was moved an estimated 35 km from Rumicolca
claims.quote: These stones were moved an estimated 35 km (22 miles) from Rumicolca.

claims.claim: The card 3 image is 'Fortress of Sacsahuamán', c. 1940, public domain
claims.quote: Archive title: File:Fortress of Sacsahuamán, Cuzco, Peru.tif ... Date: circa 1940 ... Licence: Public domain

claims.claim: A chronicler counted 20,000 men on the works
claims.quote: The Inca ordered that the provinces should provide 20,000 men and that the villages should send the necessary provisions.

claims.claim: Cieza de León wrote in 1553
claims.quote: Spanish Chronicler Pedro Cieza de León wrote in 1553:

claims.claim: 4,000 labourers quarried the stone and 6,000 conveyed it with great cables of leather and cabuya
claims.quote: There were 4,000 labourers whose duty it was to quarry and get out the stones; 6,000 conveyed them by means of great cables of leather and of cabuya[202] to the works.

claims.claim: The foundations were cut into the living rock
claims.quote: The living rock was excavated for the foundation, which was prepared with such solidity that it will endure as long as the world itself.

claims.claim: Cieza de León wrote the base was prepared so solidly "that it will endure as long as the world itself"
claims.quote: which was prepared with such solidity that it will endure as long as the world itself

claims.claim: Colonial Cuzco was built from Sacsayhuamán's stone
claims.quote: The site was destroyed block by block to salvage materials with which to build the new Spanish governmental and religious buildings of the colonial city, as well as the houses of the wealthiest Spaniards.

claims.claim: Only blocks too heavy to move remain
claims.quote: Today, it is mostly the pre-colonial stones that were too large to be easily moved that remain at the site.

claims.claim: Modern replication tests had limited success
claims.quote: An experiment was done to see if this would work on a small scale; this accomplished limited success.

claims.claim: The card 6 image is Fernando Garreaud's north-east view, 1900
claims.quote:

Date: 1900
Author: Fernando Garreaud

claims.claim: Sacsayhuamán sits at an altitude of 3,701 m
claims.quote: sits at an altitude of 3,701 metres (12,142 ft)

claims.claim: The site has three great terrace walls
claims.quote: The best-known zone of Sacsayhuamán includes its great plaza and its adjacent three massive terrace walls.

claims.claim: Pedro Pizarro wrote that "the point of a pin could not have been inserted in one of the joints"
claims.quote: they were so close together, and so well fitted, that the point of a pin could not have been inserted in one of the joints

claims.claim: The longest wall is about 400 m and around 6 m tall
claims.quote: The longest of the three walls is about 400 meters. They are about 6 meters tall.

claims.claim: The stonework totals over 6,000 cubic metres
claims.quote: The estimated volume of stone is over 6,000 cubic meters.

claims.claim: After the siege of Cusco the Spanish used the site as a quarry, taking it apart block by block
claims.quote: Following the siege of Cusco, the Spaniards began to use Sacsayhuamán as a source of stones for building Spanish Cuzco; within a few years, they had taken apart and demolished much of the complex.

claims.claim: Garcilaso de la Vega, 1609: "there is indeed not a house in the city that has not been made of this stone."
claims.quote: There is indeed not a house in the city that has not been made of this stone, or at least the houses built by the Spaniards.

claims.claim: Vince Lee is an architect
claims.quote: Vince Lee is an author, architect and explorer who has been consulted on various ancient sites that moved large megaliths.

claims.claim: Vince Lee proposed the blocks were carved first, towed up ramps and lowered into prepared pockets on stacks of logs, removed one at a time
claims.quote: Then they would be towed up a ramp and above the wall where they would be placed on top of a stack of logs. Then the logs would be removed 1 at a time to lower the stones into place carefully.

claims.claim: The experiments were never done at the scale of the largest stones
claims.quote:
the largest megaliths currently there were more than twice his estimates of the largest 
megaliths in his time

claims.claim: Surface pottery puts the earliest occupation of the hill at about 900 CE
claims.quote: Archeological studies of surface collections of pottery at Sacsayhuamán indicate that the earliest occupation of the hilltop dates to about 900 CE.

claims.claim: Ruins found at the periphery in 2008 appear ceremonial, but their exact function remains unknown
claims.quote: On 13 March 2008, archaeologists discovered additional ruins at the periphery of Sacsayhuamán. ... While appearing ceremonial in nature, the exact function remains unknown.
